overview: The Kazakh Khanate emerged from the post-Mongol steppe world in the fifteenth century and became a major Central Asian power. Its rulers governed mobile pastoral communities and competed for southern towns. “Quazaq” is this map’s spelling of Kazakh. The imported 1530 to 1783 span is neither its full lifetime nor a period of uniform control: the broad outline conceals changing alliances, contested towns and several regional khans.

sections.title: Building and governing a steppe power

items.text: Kasym Khan strengthened Kazakh power in the early sixteenth century, before this map begins. His successors faced serious internal conflicts, followed by renewed expansion under Hak-Nazar. Southern towns mattered because control of grazing country and control of markets were connected. Rival khans repeatedly fought for the oases along the Syr Darya.

In 1598, Tauekel’s army seized several southern cities but failed to take Bukhara. He died after being wounded. The subsequent settlement left Tashkent, Sairam and Turkestan with the Kazakhs, while Samarkand was relinquished. A large campaign could therefore end in negotiation and a reshaped frontier, rather than permanent possession of everything an army reached.

The Senior, Middle and Junior juz were large regional groupings, each with its own leaders. Their origins cannot be pinned to a securely documented founding ceremony. By the later khanate, a single coloured area on a map hides overlapping loyalties and rulers whose authority depended on cooperation with other influential people. Dzungar attacks from 1723 forced many Kazakhs to flee toward neighbouring territories, creating a human crisis and encouraging rulers to seek outside protection.

A bi was a judge valued for knowledge of customary law and persuasive speech. Traditions associated with Tauke Khan describe an oral body of rules covering disputes, marriage and other obligations. Scholars reconstruct this system partly from later accounts, so a neat modern “law code” would give the wrong impression of how rules were remembered and argued.

sections.title: Moving home and making a living

items.text: Pastoral households used different grazing areas through the seasons. Winter shelter, spring growth and summer pasture created a working calendar for people and animals. Herds supplied food, transport and materials, and animals could be exchanged for goods. Moving was skilled economic planning, with familiar destinations, rather than simply wandering until somewhere looked pleasant.

Early-sixteenth-century writer Ruzbihan described both portable dwellings and impressive homes mounted on carts. Some elite wagons had wooden walls, felt coverings and windows, and were pulled by camels. Smaller dwellings served ordinary herders. For some travellers, “moving house” was almost literal: the house came along for the ride.

Summer gatherings could also be social occasions. Muhatova’s study, citing Ruzbihan’s early-sixteenth-century account, describes weddings, horse races, wrestling and contests involving singers and storytellers on the summer pastures. The pastoral year made room for celebration as well as work, although this account does not describe every family or every region.

In a letter received in 1772, Abulfeiz explained that a blocked route toward Tashkent had interrupted supplies. He specifically needed flour and rice. This is a useful correction to a picture of steppe meals made entirely from meat and milk: pastoral communities also depended on agricultural neighbours and safe trading routes.

Cloth shopping had strong opinions attached. In 1773, traders complained through Abulfeiz that they had been pushed into exchanging animals for fabrics they did not want. Qing records show demand for white and red cotton. The historian relates these colours to shrouds and clothing, and to wedding textiles. A bolt of cloth could matter at several turning points in family life.

sections.title: Water, schools and life in southern towns

items.text: Sauran belonged to the southern urban world contested by Kazakh and neighbouring rulers. Its farms used both surface channels and kariz, underground galleries that collected groundwater. Summer shortages made this especially valuable: spring streams alone could not reliably supply fields and gardens through the hottest part of the year.

Aerial photographs helped researchers identify chains of kariz traces around Sauran. Combining archaeology with geology showed that Sauran and nearby Mirtobe had separate water systems. That finding challenged an older reading of a written description. Archaeology can correct a famous traveller as well as illustrate one.

Sauran’s excavated madrasa had a courtyard surrounded by small residential rooms, a teaching hall and an entrance marked by two minarets. Excavators identify it with a school described in 1515. It was built before this map’s opening year and before later Kazakh control: the khanate inherited an urban tradition of learning, rather than inventing all of its buildings.

The school’s remains preserve practical details as well as grand architecture. Rooms had wall niches and brick floors. Later occupants installed stoves with flues running through raised platforms, changing the original floor arrangement. These alterations show people adapting rooms to everyday needs; the report does not establish one exact year for each modification.

A 1769 letter from Abulfeyz Sultan to the Qing military governor includes “تيم قوانديم”, transcribed tim quwandïm and translated by its editors as “I was rather pleased.” This is Turki in Arabic script, shown here in modern typesetting from the scholarly edition. He was responding to an imperial document about travel and negotiation over territory. It is a specific diplomatic voice, not a sample of modern standard Kazakh.

Kazakh correspondence crossed several language boundaries. Some letters used Turki; others used Oirat and its Clear Script. Envoys also explained matters in person because Qing officials did not always understand the written Turkic documents fully. A letter, its seal and a messenger’s spoken explanation could work together to carry a ruler’s message.

Diplomacy did not mean that the khans simply obeyed every foreign demand. In 1775, Ablai requested Qing troops while offering revenue claimed from Tashkent. Qing officials refused and disputed the terms of his proposal. Such exchanges reveal bargaining, competing claims and sharp disagreement behind the polite titles used in official letters.

Abulkhair and a group of supporters took an oath to Russia in 1731. The relationship did not instantly place every Kazakh community under direct Russian administration. The parties had different ambitions, and later imperial expansion involved further political pressure and administrative changes. The eighteenth-century khanate cannot be reduced to a single all-or-nothing moment of “joining”.

After the map ends, Russian reforms abolished the khan’s office in the Middle juz in 1822 and the Junior juz in 1824. New districts and officials replaced important parts of regional government. These were losses of political authority, not the disappearance of Kazakh families, language or cultural life, which continued under changed and increasingly colonial conditions.

ending.text: The map stops in 1783, but Kazakh khans and communities continued. Russian expansion gradually dismantled regional khanly institutions, including reforms in 1822 and 1824. There was no single nationwide fall in 1783, and Kazakh cultural and community life survived the loss of sovereignty.
